newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says vets can sue Community in national courts.
newsitem.headline: Court says vets can sue Community in national courts.

text.p: The European Court of Justice on Tuesday granted standing to individuals to challenge Community institutions in national courts for violating the Common Agricultural Policy.
The court said individuals could raise the legal principles of non-discrimination and proportionality to attack the application of Community rules in the agricultural sector.
However, the court refused to throw out the Council directive requiring slaughterhouse inspections of meat traded in the Community, after a challenge from British slaughterhouse operators.

The operators, Bakers of Nailsea, argued the law's requirement for on site ante-mortem inspections by veterinarian surgeons places an undue burden on their business, as they must pay for the inspections.

Bakers told the court the costs should be borne by the public as they benefit from the free trade of goods insured by the inspection requirements. The court distinguished previous decisions upon which the Bakers based this argument, noting that those cases involved fines unilaterally imposed by member states, and not an EU law meant to harmonize Community rules.
The court also rejected Bakers argument that an ante-mortem inspection by an official veterinarian was unjustified and excessive.

"The Community institutions enjoy a wide discretionary power regarding not only establishment of the factual basis of their action but also definition of the objective to be pursued, within the framework of the treaty, and choice of the appropriate action," the court said.
"Ante-mortem health inspections in slaughterhouses - Role of official veterinarians - Charges passed on to slaughterhouses operators"
Reference from the High Court of Justice (Bristol Mercantile Court, UK) between
Woodspring District Council and Bakers of Nailsea Ltd

on the validity of Council directive 64/443 on health problems affecting intra-Community trade in fresh meat, articles 39 and 40(3) of the EC treaty and the general principles of proportionality and non-discrimination

1. A private individual may plead in proceedings before a national court an infringement of articles 39 and 40(3) of the EC treaty and of the general principles of proportionality and non-discrimination in order to challenge the validity of an act of the Community institutions.

2. Council directive 64/443 on health problems affecting intra-Community trade in fresh meat is not invalid having regard to articles 39 and 40(3) of the EC treaty and the general principles of proportionality, in so far as it requires and/or permits member state to require health inspections at slaughterhouses to be carried out by official veterinarians and/or in so far as it requires ante-mortem inspections to be carried out.

3. The obligation under directve 64/433 for the costs of health inspections by official veterinarians to be borne by the slaughterhouse at which the animals are to be slaughtered is not contrary either to articles 39 and 40(3) of the EC treaty or to the general principals of equal treatment and/or proportionality.
